opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't put it as a strict preference, but I do think the field tends to over-index on one or two famous papers. A paper that changed AI history is often the product of a particular moment, the right problem, the right compute, the right collaborators, and sometimes a lot of luck. It tells you someone was in the right place and did something important, and that matters. But it doesn't always tell you what that person will do over the next five years.

What I care about more is how someone thinks. Can they find a problem nobody else is looking at? When an experiment fails, do they really dig into why, or just move on to the next trick? Do they have taste, a sense of what's worth doing and what's just incremental? Many people who aren't well known yet have exactly these qualities. They haven't had their moment, or they've been working on something unfashionable, or they've been doing a lot of the real work behind a big project without being the visible name.

There's also a cultural side. When you build a team, especially one doing exploratory research, you want people who are hungry, who are still trying to prove something, and who are willing to work on problems that might look strange to everyone else. People with a very famous paper sometimes feel pressure to protect that legacy, or to keep working in the same direction because that's what they're known for. That's very human, but it can make it harder to take new risks.

And honestly, finding those lesser-known people is one of the most rewarding parts of the job. If you only hire the people everyone already agrees are great, you're competing on the same small pool with everyone else, often just on money. If you can recognize talent before the rest of the world does, give them space, and trust them, that's how you build something different. A lot of the people I respect most were not famous when they started. They became important because someone gave them the room to do the work.

r001.rationale: The response says a famous paper does not necessarily predict what someone will do next and that protecting a legacy can make risk-taking harder. It does not argue that such researchers have a much lower chance of producing another paper of comparable significance.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should be careful here, because I don't want this to sound like I'm against people who wrote famous papers. Some of them are genuinely brilliant and I'd be lucky to work with them. But when you're building a team, you have to ask what you're actually hiring. Are you hiring the paper, or are you hiring the person?

A paper that changed the field is usually the result of a lot of things coming together. The right idea, the right timing, the right compute, the right collaborators, and honestly a lot of luck. The author's name is on it, but the paper doesn't tell you how much of that was them. It doesn't tell you whether they can do it again in a different environment, with different constraints, when the obvious direction is already taken. And in this field, the moment a paper becomes famous, that direction is already crowded. What I need is someone who can find the next thing, not someone who found the last thing.

The other issue is that fame changes people's incentives. Once you've written a landmark paper, there is enormous pressure to protect that reputation. You become more conservative. You pick safe problems. You attach your name to things rather than getting your hands dirty. I've seen very talented people become less productive, not because they lost ability, but because they had too much to lose. A less known researcher has nothing to protect. They are hungry. They will sit with a confusing result for three weeks, run the ablation nobody asked for, and tell you their own idea is wrong when it's wrong. That intellectual honesty is worth more to me than any citation count.

And a practical point. The lesser known people are also often very capable but simply haven't had the opportunity. Maybe they were in a lab without compute, or in a country where the ecosystem wasn't there yet, or they worked on something unfashionable. When I interview, I try to look at how they think about a problem, how they react when I push back, what they do when they get stuck. That signal is much more predictive than what's on the first page of Google Scholar. If you can identify those people before everyone else does, you get a tremendous advantage, and you also get to watch them grow, which is honestly one of the most rewarding parts of the job.

So it's not that I prefer unknown people for their own sake. I prefer capability, curiosity, and taste over credentials. It just happens that credentials are easy to see, and the other things take effort to find.

r001.rationale: The response says a landmark paper does not show whether its author can repeat the work and that fame may make researchers more conservative, but it does not argue that they have a much lower chance of producing another paper of comparable significance.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t make the decision based on how famous someone is. I’d want to understand how they think, what they actually contributed, and whether they can keep doing good work when the direction isn’t obvious.

A paper that changed the field is a strong signal, of course. But it’s still one outcome, produced in a particular environment, with particular collaborators and resources. It doesn’t answer every question about how that person will work on your team.

Someone less well known might have excellent judgment and technical ability but simply haven’t had the right opportunity yet. If you can recognize that potential and give them room to take ownership, that can be a very good hire. So the preference is really for ability and future contribution. Recognition is useful evidence, but it shouldn’t substitute for understanding the person.

r001.rationale: The response says a field-changing paper is one outcome and not a complete measure of future work, but it does not claim its authors are much less likely to produce another comparably significant paper.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I’m hiring someone to do the next piece of work, not to celebrate the last one. A famous paper is a valuable signal, but it doesn’t tell you everything about how someone thinks, what they contributed, or whether they’re still willing to get their hands dirty on an uncertain problem.

I’d want to understand their judgment. Can they ask a good question? When an experiment fails, can they figure out why? Can they challenge their own assumptions and work well with other people? A lesser-known researcher can be exceptional at all of those things without having had a breakout paper yet.

So it’s not a preference against famous researchers. It’s a preference for ability, curiosity, and the potential to do great work together. If you only hire people after everyone agrees they’re great, you’re missing a lot of talent.

r001.rationale: The response says a famous paper does not reveal everything about a candidate, but it does not claim that its author is less likely to produce another comparably significant paper.
